analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a flat 10% tax on wages, while ending all taxes on corporations, estates, and investment income.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee; it was introduced in January 1991 and died without a hearing, vote, or cosponsors beyond one House Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the corporate income tax, the estate and gift taxes, and every tax on life insurers, mutual funds, real estate trusts, and foreign corporations doing business in the U.S. [S2]. It would replace the individual income tax with a flat 10% levy on earned income — wages, salaries, and self-employment earnings — above a $10,000 exemption, while income from investments, capital gains, and interest would be taxed not at all [S2][S3]. It would also wipe out all tax deductions and credits, including the earned income credit and the mortgage deduction, and grant amnesty to anyone who owed back income taxes before 1990 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations, insurance companies, mutual funds, real estate trusts, and foreign corporations would stop paying federal income taxes entirely. Wealthy households would pay no tax on capital gains, interest, or rents, and no estate or gift tax on inherited wealth. Anyone with unpaid back taxes before 1990 would have the debt forgiven [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the corporate income tax, the corporate alternative minimum tax, and specialized taxes on life insurers, mutual insurance companies, regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, mutual savings banks, and foreign corporations with U.S. business income [S2][S3].
It repeals the estate tax, the gift tax, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, so large inheritances would pass untaxed [S2][S3].

Only 'earned income' — wages, salaries, self-employment earnings, and compensation paid as dividends — would be taxed at 10% above a $10,000 exemption. Capital gains, interest, rents, and other investment income are not on the list and would be tax-free [S3].
It grants amnesty for all income tax liability, penalties, and interest for taxable years ending before 1990, except money already paid and tax tied to illegal activity [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary wage earners would carry nearly the whole federal income tax load: a flat 10% on wages above $10,000, with every deduction and credit — the earned income credit, child benefits, the mortgage interest deduction, retirement savings credits — repealed. Large families would lose more than they gained from the flat $10,000 exemption. The federal government would also lose most of its corporate and estate tax revenue, forcing spending cuts, new taxes, or more debt [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Repealing all individual deductions and credits would hit working families hardest: the earned income credit, child-related benefits, and the mortgage interest deduction would all disappear, while the flat $10,000 exemption helps a single filer far more than a parent supporting several children [S2][S3].

Because only earned income is taxed, a person living on capital gains, interest, or rents would owe nothing, while a worker earning the same amount would pay 10% above $10,000 — a large shift of the tax burden from wealth to work [S3].
Retirees' pension and annuity income would be exempt, meaning a retiree with substantial income could pay no tax while a full-time worker with modest wages pays [S3].

Repealing the corporate income tax, estate tax, and taxes on insurers, mutual funds, and foreign corporations would remove a major share of federal revenue at once, with no replacement revenue beyond the flat wage tax [S2].
The amnesty would forgive all unpaid income taxes, penalties, and interest owed for years before 1990 by people who simply never paid [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers simplicity — a 10% flat rate with a $10,000 exemption — but pays for it by eliminating all taxes on corporations, estates, and investment income, while repealing the deductions and credits working families rely on. It would shift the income tax almost entirely onto wages and salaries, with the largest gains flowing to corporations, heirs of large estates, and people living on investment income. The back-tax amnesty adds a further giveaway. Any honest weighing finds the costs to wage earners and to federal revenue far larger than the benefit of a simpler tax form.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or moved it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the Crane Tithe Tax Act of 1991 on January 3, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
One House Republican cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: the Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, the House never voted on it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary wage earners and the federal Treasury came out ahead, because a bill that would have shifted the income tax onto wages, ended corporate and estate taxes, and forgiven unpaid back taxes never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Philip Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and titled it the Crane Tithe Tax Act of 1991.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it, held no recorded action, and let it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted only its Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how parties would have split.

industries.industry: Corporations and foreign companies with U.S. business income
industries.note: The bill repeals the corporate income tax, the corporate minimum tax, and the tax on foreign corporations' U.S. income entirely. The revenue those taxes raise would fall on wage earners instead.

Estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would be repealed, and investment income such as capital gains and interest would not be taxed at all under the new levy. Back taxes owed before 1990 would be forgiven.
Special taxes on life, mutual, and other insurance companies would be repealed, ending their federal income tax while their customers' wage taxes remain.

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The taxes on regulated investment companies and REITs would be repealed, making these investment vehicles fully tax-sheltered.
The alternative tax on mutual savings banks would be repealed along with the rest of corporate taxation.
